kakekotoba.interaction: Ikuno is a real place name on the road to Tango, but 'iku' simultaneously evokes 行く 'to go,' reinforcing the sense of a long road being traveled/journeyed — the place name and the verb of travel are fused.

kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 踏み (to step/tread, from 踏む, echoing 道 'road' and place name Ikuno)
kakekotoba.interaction: The poem's ostensible surface message is 'I have not yet received a letter,' but ふみ also echoes 踏み, the treading of the road just described in the kami-no-ku — the walked road and the awaited letter are bound together in one word, so that the physical distance of the road stands for the impossibility of yet having a letter.

jokotoba.text: 大江山いく野の道のとほければ
jokotoba.pivot: ふみ (via the echo with 踏み, and the general sense of the long road)
jokotoba.function: The entire kami-no-ku describes a real, extremely long physical road (from Kyoto through Oeyama and Ikuno to Tango province) purely in order to establish 'とほければ' (being far/long), which then pivots via associative imagery/kakekotoba into the shimo-no-ku's claim about not yet having received a letter (ふみ) nor set foot on (ふみ) the road to Ama no Hashidate.

honkadori.source_poem: Ise Monogatari-associated or general konkyo of famous uta-makura places (Oeyama, Ikuno, Ama no Hashidate)
honkadori.function: This poem is itself famous as an impromptu retort composed on the spot (in the celebrated anecdote of Fujiwara no Sadayori's teasing) rather than as an allusion to a prior fixed poem; no single earlier honka can be identified with confidence, so this field records the traditional association rather than a verified textual source.

kigo.note: Ama no Hashidate is a famous scenic place (meisho) rather than a seasonal word; the poem is built entirely around place names (Oeyama, Ikuno, Ama no Hashidate) functioning as uta-makura, with no seasonal image present. The poem's power lies in geographic/rhetorical wit rather than seasonal association.

bipartite.kami_theme: The great length and remoteness of the actual physical road from the capital through Oeyama and Ikuno toward Tango province
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker's witty denial that she has yet received any letter from her mother, nor set foot on that road herself, refuting an insinuation that her poems were ghostwritten
bipartite.pivot_note: The poem is a rhetorical rebuttal built as a single extended conceit: the kami-no-ku establishes the literal distance and difficulty of the road to Tango (where the speaker's mother lived), and the shimo-no-ku pivots on the kakekotoba ふみ (letter/treading) to claim, in effect, 'the road is so far that I have neither traveled it nor received a letter by it' — simultaneously a literal geographic statement and a pointed retort defending her poetic authorship. This is best classified as 'other': the relationship is argumentative/rhetorical rather than seasonal, causal-physical, or a simple visual revelation, since the entire poem functions as wordplay-driven proof within an anecdote.
